**The Whispering Shadows of the Forgotten**

---

### **I. The First Light**

The world was not always dark. Not in the way it is now, when the sky bleeds into twilight like a wound that never heals. Long ago, there was light—soft, golden, the kind that lingers in the corners of a room long after the sun has set. The stars were bright, not distant pinpricks, but living things, pulsing with their own quiet energy. The rivers ran clear, the forests hummed with unseen voices, and the earth itself seemed to breathe.

But then came the change.

One night, the sky split open. Not with thunder, not with fire, but with a sound like a thousand voices speaking at once—high and low, sharp and mournful. The light dimmed. The stars flickered, then vanished. The rivers turned black, their waters thick with something that slithered beneath the surface, unseen. The forests stood silent, their leaves drooping as if in sorrow. And the people? They did not know why.

They called it the *Great Silence*. The world had forgotten how to speak.

---

### **II. The Hollow Men**

They came in the twilight.

Not as monsters, not as gods—just… people. But different. Their eyes were too wide, their mouths stretched into silent grins. They walked with a slow, deliberate step, as if each step were a prayer. Some carried things—rusted tools, broken toys, the bones of animals. Others carried nothing at all, just the weight of something unseen.

The first time I saw them, I was twelve years old, standing at the edge of the old mill pond. The water was still, too still. And then—there they were.

Three of them. Two men, one woman. The woman’s hair was white as snow, her fingers long and bony. The men wore tattered clothes, their faces painted with strange symbols. They did not speak. They did not need to.

I ran.

But the pond was not kind. The water rose around me, cold and hungry. I screamed, but my voice was swallowed by the silence. Then, from the depths, something *moved*. Not a fish. Not a creature. Something that had been there all along, waiting.

I woke up in the woods, my clothes torn, my hands raw. The sky was still dark, but the air smelled different—like wet stone and old paper. I did not tell anyone what I had seen. Not even my mother.

---

### **III. The Book of Lost Names**

They say the Hollow Men take names.

Not just any name. The name of a person who still remembers the light. A child who still believes in the stars. A heart that still beats with something other than fear.

I found the book in the attic.

It was old. The pages were yellowed, the ink smudged. The title was scratched in the corner: *"The Names We Forgot."* Inside, there were lists. Names of people who had lived before the Great Silence. Some were famous—poets, kings, scientists. Others were just ordinary, like my grandmother’s name, *Elara Veyne*, who had died in the war before the sky fell.

But the worst part was the last entry.

*"Liam Carter. Age 12. Last seen near the mill pond."*

I had forgotten his name. I had forgotten his face. But the Hollow Men had not.

That night, I dreamed of him.

He was standing at the edge of the pond again. But this time, he was smiling. His eyes were black, like the water, but they were *happy*. He reached for me, and when I woke up, my hands were cold, my fingers tingling.

---

### **IV. The Bridge of Whispers**

The Hollow Men do not walk in straight lines.

They follow paths that are not meant to be followed. They lead you to places where the air is thick with something you cannot see. Where the trees grow in unnatural patterns, where the ground is soft as velvet beneath your feet.

I followed one such path one evening, drawn by a sound like wind through dead leaves. It led me to a bridge—no, not a bridge, but something older. The wood was black, the stones worn smooth by time. And on the other side, the water was still, but the surface rippled with shapes that shifted when you looked away.

The Hollow Men were waiting.

There were five of them. Two men, two women, and one child—no older than ten. The child’s face was smooth, like a baby’s, but its eyes were too big. It did not speak. It did not need to.

The woman with white hair held out a hand. "Come," she said. "The light is waiting."

I wanted to run. But the child was looking at me, and I knew—if I left now, they would find me again. So I stepped forward.

The bridge dissolved beneath my feet. I was standing in a place that was not a place at all. A space between worlds. The Hollow Men were gone. But the child was still there, smiling.

"You remember me," it said.

I did not answer.

---

### **V. The Weight of Silence**

They say the Hollow Men do not take names from the living. They take them from the dead.

From the ones who have forgotten.

From the ones who have stopped believing.

From the ones who have stopped *living*.

I have seen it happen.

A man who had lost his wife in the war. He would wake up in the night, his hands clenched around a photograph, his face wet with tears. The Hollow Men would come to him in his dreams, whispering his name. And when he woke, the photograph would be gone. His wife’s name would be erased from the book.

A child who had lost her father. She would scream in her sleep, but no one would hear. The Hollow Men would take her name, and when she woke, she would forget why she had cried.

And me?

I have forgotten too much.

I have forgotten the taste of rain on my skin. I have forgotten the sound of my mother’s voice. I have forgotten the name of the boy who used to sit beside me on the train.

But the Hollow Men do not take my name.

Not yet.

---

### **VI. The Last Light**

The sky is not dark anymore.

Not entirely.

There are patches of it—flickering, like candle flames in a draft. Sometimes, if you look hard enough, you can see them. Small, bright, and *alive*. They do not stay long. They come and go like ghosts.

The Hollow Men say they are the last remnants of the old world. That they are trying to remember what was lost.

But I think they are lying.

I think they are trying to *keep* it.

Because the light is not enough.

The light is not enough to fill the hollow places in our hearts. The light is not enough to make us remember.

But the Hollow Men are not afraid of the dark.

They are afraid of the silence.

And that is why they are here.

---

### **VII. The Choice**

I have made my choice.

I will not let them take my name.

I will not let them take my memories.

I will not let them take the light from me.

But I will not fight them either.

Because they are not monsters. They are not villains. They are just… people.

People who have lost everything.

People who are trying to find their way back.

And maybe, just maybe, they need us to help them.

So I will walk the paths they lead me to. I will listen to the whispers in the wind. I will remember the names of the forgotten.

Because if we do not remember, they will never be able to find their way back either.

---

### **VIII. The End (Or Is It?)**

The book of lost names is still open.

The last entry is still there.

*"Liam Carter. Age 12. Last seen near the mill pond."*

I do not know if he is still alive. I do not know if he remembers me.

But I will keep looking.

Because the world is not over.

The light is not gone.

And maybe, just maybe, one day, the sky will remember how to shine again.

---

**The End.**

*(Or perhaps, just the beginning.)*
